problem: VLMs ground open-vocabulary phrases well but cannot reliably output metric quantities (range, bearing, comparative spatial relations). Existing fixes either fold geometry into a hand-engineered per-robot pipeline or ask the model for waypoints, and both require rewriting the control stack for each new robot, task or vocabulary.
motivation: Real-world robots must follow language instructions, find referred objects and answer spatial questions in unseen buildings without a prebuilt map or fixed vocabulary. The authors observe that a VLM can ground 'the lantern closest to the fan decoration' but still invents ranges or picks the wrong comparative, and that it tends to return the anchor when asked for the closest candidate. They therefore treat the failure as an interface problem and enforce a boundary in which the VLM supplies semantics and geometry supplies metres.
key_idea: Expose the perception and navigation stack as a Model Context Protocol tool server whose tools accept only phrases and opaque handles, never numbers, so the VLM proposes semantics while LiDAR-based geometry and a controller model decide all metrics.
insight: The scan-based lift is far more accurate than the model's own distance (the paper reports a lower median absolute range error), and it decides object reference outright (10/45 hits vs 0/45 for model-emitted coordinates). Yet it is almost invisible in navigation, because the platform re-plans every waypoint against its own terrain map. What costs navigation score is not knowing where the waypoint will settle: removing the platform model drops the score by 13.3 points (t=2.77), while removing the lift is not resolved and mainly saves grounding calls. Removing the tool structure while keeping perception barely changes object-reference hit rate, so the schema itself is not the load-bearing part. The tools it wraps (explore, expand_vocab) change what the scene graph holds.
method: Handle-typed MCP interface: 10 tools (ground, expand_vocab, verify_present, nearest, farthest, between, drive_to, explore, orbit, publish). Every input is a phrase or an opaque handle such as obj_7 that the server issued. No tool accepts metres or radians, so model-invented coordinates cannot reach the robot.

ground (VLM plus LiDAR lift): unwraps the equirectangular panorama into overlapping gnomonic faces and asks the VLM for boxes. Each box centre is unprojected to a bearing, and the median range of LiDAR returns in a narrow cone becomes depth. Three gates (elevation floor, implied-size check, empty-cone test) can refuse the lift; a refused handle is marked unmeasured, and drive_to on it steps a bounded distance along the bearing.

Comparative tools: nearest, farthest and between are arithmetic over the persistent object graph rather than client judgement, so they range over every instance ever seen. between returns a passage midpoint.

Persistent object graph (following SysNav): YOLOv8x-World v2 detects on four gnomonic faces and SAM 2.1 Hiera-L refines masks. Each mask is lifted to a metric 3D box using LiDAR returns and folded into identity-keyed records. expand_vocab and verify_present control the searched vocabulary.

Controller model in drive_to: reimplements the unmodifiable autonomy stack's objective against the same terrain map, predicts where the vehicle will rest, and publishes the waypoint whose predicted resting place is nearest the target handle. Arrival is a distance test on odometry. Porting to another platform replaces only this model.

explore and orbit: explore drives to the frontier of unseen space when a phrase will not resolve, to grow the graph. orbit walks an arc around a reached handle to tighten its 3D extent. publish outputs the graph-committed 3D box.

Instruction decomposition: an instruction is split once into ordered clauses (destinations, keep-outs, passages) so later comparatives can refer to an anchor set by an earlier clause. The reasoning client is Claude Opus 5.

setting.backbone: Claude Opus 5 (frozen MCP client, extended thinking disabled) plus YOLOv8x-World v2 and SAM 2.1 Hiera-Large (frozen perception)
setting.observation: 360° equirectangular RGB (1920x640, 2 Hz), registered LiDAR scan, terrain map, odometry
setting.action_space: single Pose2D waypoint to an external autonomy stack (/way_point_with_heading), chosen via handle-based tool calls
setting.simulator: CMU VLN Challenge 2026 simulator (unspecified in the text), ROS interface
setting.privileged: none stated (no prebuilt map; starts from a fixed pose)

numbers.eval_set_note: development set, all instruction-following questions over all scenes (about 30 questions, implied by df=29)
numbers.extra: authors' own reimplementation of the scoring protocol (closed official evaluator); 10 min per question; 1.25 m arrival tolerance
numbers.evidence: Abstract: 'The full system achieves 64.4% on instruction following, dropping by 13.3 percentage points without controller modeling (t=2.77)'

numbers.eval_set_note: frozen set of 45 comparative referring questions on the same development scenes
numbers.extra: hit = 3D IoU above the challenge overlap threshold; scoring rule implemented by authors
numbers.evidence: Abstract: 'clears the challenge's overlap threshold on 10 of 45 questions (versus 0 of 45 ...), reducing median center error from 3.37 m to 2.48 m'

numbers_note: The LaTeX source uses unresolved macros for most table values (e.g. \armOurs, \ndtwOurs, \tlrOurs, \ttFullPct), so Tables 2-4 are not readable. Only the numbers printed in the abstract are recorded. nDTW, TL ratio and closest-approach values for the arms are not available.
results: The full system scores 64.4% on instruction following, and removing the controller/platform model costs 13.3 points (t=2.77), while removing the lift is not resolved. On object reference it reaches 10/45 hits with median centre error 2.48 m, against 0/45 hits and 3.37 m when the model emits coordinates itself. No published system is compared; only the authors' own ablations serve as baselines.
limitations: Latency is high: about half a minute per model call and step, because every tool waits on a round trip to a frontier model.

Evaluation uses one simulator, one robot and one frontier model, with no real hardware. The portability claim for the controller model is untested, and it is unknown whether the handle boundary matters more for weaker models.

The official evaluator is closed, so the arrival tolerance and instance-matching rule are the authors' own. Only the development set is used, the sample is small (about 30 IF and 45 object-reference questions) with substantial run-to-run noise, and the absolute object-reference hit rate is modest (10/45).
